meta.blurb: While the roads out of London fill with people fleeing the plague, saddler HF opens his Bible and decides to stay. In 1665 he sees red crosses on doors, silent streets, great pits and neighbours who risk their lives to help.
meta.bible: A Journal of the Plague Year: Daniel Defoe's book, published in 1722; the narrator is imagined, and much of it follows real records. Daniel Defoe: the author, a small child in 1665. HF: the narrator, a London saddler with a house and shop outside Aldgate; he stays in the city through the plague. Aldgate: the old city gate and the district where HF lives; the great plague pit is beside Aldgate church. Whitechapel: nearby district. London: the city, with about one in five people dying in 1665. Holland: where the plague was first heard of in September 1664. Long Acre: the street near Drury Lane in the west where two men died in December 1664. Drury Lane: nearby street. Bills of Mortality: weekly printed lists of burials from the parish clerks. Searchers: old women paid to examine the dead and name the cause. Watchmen: guards at the doors of shut-up houses; houses were shut for a month and marked with a red cross and the words Lord have mercy upon us. Lord Mayor: the city's leader, who issued orders. Solomon Eagle: a man who walked the streets with a pan of burning coals on his head. Nineveh: the city in the Bible warned in forty days. Epping Forest: where three poor men camp. Thames: the river with boats and ships. The King and his court: left London in the summer and returned early in 1666. The Great Fire: burned old London in September 1666. Marseille: French port whose plague in 1720 alarmed England. Psalm 91: the psalm HF reads before deciding to stay. Voice and tone: calm, observant, plain, humane; an ordinary witness who reports and does not exaggerate; dark subjects treated factually, without gore. In the pages the narrator is written HF.

B1B2: In September 1664, a London man called HF hears that the plague has returned to Holland. Everyone in the city talks about it, and nobody can say whether the sickness will cross the sea.

The government orders ships from infected countries to be kept apart, but the danger seems far away. Londoners go on with their trade and their pleasures, because the sickness has stayed on the other side of the sea.

In December 1664, two men die of the plague in Long Acre, near Drury Lane, in the west of London. Fear spreads quickly from door to door, and people begin to wonder whether the sickness has really come.
The narrator, HF, is a saddler with a house and a shop near Aldgate, in the east of London. He decides to write down everything he sees, so that others may learn from it.
Every week the parish clerks print the Bills of Mortality, which count the dead in each parish. Londoners read the lists with growing fear, because the numbers rise as spring turns to summer.
Before the plague arrives, two comets appear in the sky over London. Many people take them as warnings of a terrible disaster, and they talk of nothing else.
Fortune tellers, astrologers and quack doctors do good business, because frightened people will pay for any promise. Printed bills on every corner offer pills, drinks and charms against the plague.
By early summer the plague has spread from the west of the city toward the east. Soon it reaches the streets around HF's own house, and he can no longer pretend that it is somebody else's trouble.
Those who can afford it leave London in coaches and carts piled high with belongings. The King and his court depart as well, and the roads out of the city are crowded with people trying to escape.
HF's brother, who lives in the country, begs him to leave the city and bring his family to safety. HF is torn, because his house, his shop and all his goods are in London.
One night HF opens his Bible and finds the ninety-first Psalm, which speaks of God's protection from pestilence. He takes it as a sign, and he decides to stay in London.
HF fills his house with bread, butter, cheese and beer so that he need not go to market. Even so, his curiosity is too strong, and he keeps walking out to see what is happening.
The Lord Mayor and his aldermen publish strict orders for the city. They appoint officers to examine the sick, watch the houses and bury the dead, and they forbid large crowds.
When someone falls ill, the whole household is shut in for a month, and a red cross is painted on the door. A watchman sits outside day and night to make sure that nobody goes in or out.
People shut inside their homes try every trick to escape, and some climb out of windows at night. Some bribe the watchmen, while others fool them with a false message or a sudden quarrel.
Old women called searchers are paid to examine every body and report the cause of death. Some are careless and some accept small bribes, so the Bills probably count fewer victims than the truth.

Believing that animals carry the sickness, the city orders its dogs and cats to be killed. Many historians now think that rats and their fleas spread the plague, so the order may have done more harm than good.
HF slowly understands that people who look healthy may carry the sickness. They can pass it to their friends and families for days before they feel ill themselves.
In the heat of the summer, the streets of London fall strangely silent. Grass begins to grow where crowds used to walk, and only a few frightened people hurry along.
When trade stops, thousands of workers and servants lose their jobs and fall into hunger. The Lord Mayor and many rich citizens give money and food, which helps many families to survive.
Many frightened Londoners move onto boats and ships in the River Thames. They hope that the water will keep them safe, and some stay there for weeks.
Some ministers flee from London, but others stay to preach and comfort the sick. Churches are half empty, and worshippers sit far apart, watching their neighbours with fear.
A man named Solomon Eagle walks through the streets with a pan of burning coals on his head. He cries out in a terrible voice about the anger of God, and frightened people hurry away from him.

The silence of the city is broken by cries from open windows, where people call out in grief. One man walks the streets crying that the city will be overthrown in forty days, as the prophet warned Nineveh.
At night, carts roll slowly through the streets while a bell rings and a voice calls out for the dead. Families lay their loved ones at the door, and the carts carry them away for burial.
The graveyards are soon full, so the parish digs great pits for the dead. HF goes to see the one near Aldgate, and the size of it shocks him.
HF tells a story he has heard about a drunken piper who fell asleep in the street one night. The men on the cart took him for dead and lifted him on, but he woke up and asked where he was.
In September the Bills record more than seven thousand deaths in a single week. HF believes that the true number is higher, because so many deaths were never counted.
Some of the sick suffer so much from fever and pain that they lose their senses. They run out into the street, and a few even run to the river.
Some families are so afraid that they leave a sick relative alone. HF also tells of neighbours who risk their own lives to bring food and comfort.
Many poor women work as nurses, taking care of the sick for small pay. HF says that some are greedy or careless, but he thinks that many are brave and deserve thanks.
HF tells a long story about three poor men who decide to leave London together. They take a little money, some tools and a few supplies, and they walk out toward the forest.
The three men find a quiet place at the edge of Epping Forest and build a rough shelter there. They keep away from other people, and they depend on the kindness of villagers for bread.
Villages and towns in the country are afraid of Londoners and set guards on the roads. Travellers need a paper to show that they are healthy, and many are turned away.
HF asks whether the plague is a punishment from God or only a natural disease. He decides that it can be both, because God can work through ordinary causes such as infection.
The watchmen, gravediggers and cart drivers are mostly poor men who need the wages. They face the sickness every day, and many of them die at their work.
Everyone is afraid of everyone else, and friends no longer shake hands when they meet. People carry herbs and perfumes in their pockets and cross the street to avoid a stranger.
HF notices that the plague does not strike every part of London at the same time. It begins in the west and then moves east, and the crowded poor parishes suffer the most.
In October the weekly number of deaths begins to fall, and people dare to hope again. HF describes how faces in the street change from fear to relief.
As autumn goes on, more and more of the sick begin to recover. HF reports that even the doctors do not agree about the reason, and he leaves the question open.
In their joy, many Londoners forget to be careful and shake hands with everyone they meet. Some even visit the sick, and a number of them fall ill and die just as hope returns.
As the sickness weakens, shopkeepers take down their shutters and the streets slowly fill with people. Families who fled in the summer return in coaches and carts, and trade begins again.
With the arrival of the cold winter weather, the plague almost disappears from London. A few cases continue into the new year, but the Bills show only small numbers now.
About 100,000 people died of the plague in London in 1665, according to the usual estimates. That was roughly one in every five people who lived in the city.
HF himself never catches the plague, even though he walked through the streets so often. He gives thanks for his survival, but he cannot say why he was spared when so many were not.
HF ends with practical advice for anyone who may face such a danger in the future. Keep supplies at home, he says, avoid crowds, ignore quack cures and help your neighbours.
In September 1666, a year after the worst of the plague, the Great Fire burns much of old London. The city is rebuilt with more brick and stone, and a plague on such a scale never visits it again.

In 1722, when plague in France had frightened England again, Defoe published the book to remind readers of the real danger. For many years afterwards, some readers believed that it was a true diary written by a real person.
Readers still enjoy the book because it shows how ordinary people behave in a time of fear. Some are selfish and some are generous, but most simply try to survive and help each other.

HF ends his journal with a short rhyme about the great plague of 1665, which swept a hundred thousand souls away. He signs himself HF, and his last line is a quiet cry of thanks that he is still alive.
C1C2: Daniel Defoe's Journal of the Plague Year, published in 1722, is narrated by an imagined London citizen called HF, and it opens in September 1664 with a rumour that the plague has returned to Holland. Defoe was only a small child during the real epidemic of 1665, so he built his book from official records, reports and the memories of those who had lived through it. Its facts are largely true to history, but the narrator and many of his stories are imagined, and the result is a vivid account of how ordinary people face a terrifying danger.

The government quickly ordered ships arriving from Holland to be kept apart for a time, but most Londoners felt that the danger lay safely across the sea. The plague had visited England before, and in the memory of old people it had always passed, so the news was soon mixed up with every other rumour of the day. Life went on, trade went on, and the city did not yet suspect how close the sickness already was.

In December 1664, two men died of the plague in Long Acre, near Drury Lane, in the western part of the city, and people quickly drew back in alarm. For a time the sickness seemed to fade, and the cold weather gave Londoners a false sense of safety. But the spark had been struck, and by the following spring it would spread through the parishes like fire through dry straw.

The narrator is a saddler who lives and works just outside Aldgate, one of the old gates in the walls of the City, in a crowded district of craftsmen and traders. He is a sensible, observant man with no special learning, and that is exactly what makes him a useful witness. As the sickness draws near his door, he resolves to set down everything he sees, so that people in some future age may know what it was like.

Each week the parish clerks collected the number of burials and published them in the printed Bills of Mortality, which every anxious Londoner learned to read like a weather report. In the early months of 1665 the figures were small, yet they crept upward, and the parishes on the western edge of the city showed the first warning signs. HF tells us that people studied the Bills with the same care that sailors give to the sky before a storm.

In the winter before the sickness took hold, two comets were seen in the sky over London, and crowds stood in the streets to stare at them. HF notes that many people took the sight as a sign of coming disaster, and the old women of the city were quick to explain what the stars meant. He himself thinks that such fears did far more harm than good, since they made people anxious long before the real danger arrived.

Quack doctors, fortune tellers and astrologers found that fear was an excellent business, and their printed bills appeared on every corner, promising pills, drinks and charms that would keep the plague away. HF is scornful of them, and he warns that many simple people trusted these cheats instead of taking real care, and so exposed themselves to danger. The more frightened a person became, he observes, the more eagerly he would believe anything he was told by a confident voice.

As spring turned to summer, the sickness crept from the western parishes toward the crowded streets of the east, and the weekly numbers in the Bills began to climb alarmingly. Soon it was knocking at the doors around HF's own house, and he could no longer tell himself that the danger belonged to other people. Around him the whole city seemed to hold its breath, waiting to learn whose house would be next.

As the numbers climbed, everyone who could afford it fled: merchants, gentlemen, lawyers and even the King and his court, whose coaches and carts crowded the roads out of the city. Those who stayed behind watched the great houses fall silent, with their shutters closed and their servants dismissed, one street after another. The people who could not leave were the poor, for they had neither money nor refuge, and they were left to face the plague almost alone.

HF's brother, who had already carried his own family away to safety in the country, wrote urgently and begged him to follow without delay. The saddler was deeply torn, for everything he owned was tied up in his house, his shop and his goods, and to abandon them seemed like ruin. Day after day he weighed one danger against another, and the longer he waited, the harder it became to leave.

At the height of his doubts, HF picked up his Bible and read the ninety-first Psalm, with its promise that those who trust in God will be delivered from the deadly pestilence. He understood these words as a message meant for himself, and a strange calm came over him as he read. From that hour he resolved to remain in London, though he admits that other readers may judge his choice a foolish one, and that he did not urge it on anyone else.

Having chosen to stay, HF set about preparing his household, and he laid in a stock of bread, butter, cheese and beer so that his servants would not have to visit the markets too often. He meant to keep himself safely indoors, but he was an inquisitive man, and he found that he could not bear to sit at home while history happened outside. Again and again he ventured into the streets, and it is because of those walks that we have his remarkable record.

The Lord Mayor and his aldermen, to their credit, remained in the city and issued a series of detailed orders to fight the plague. Officers called examiners, searchers and watchmen were appointed in every parish, while public feasts, plays and crowded gatherings in taverns were forbidden. HF approves of the aim of these measures, although he sees clearly that they often fell hardest on the poor.

Perhaps the most feared of all the orders was the one that shut up every infected house, with the healthy and the sick locked in together for a month. A red cross was painted on the door, together with the words Lord have mercy upon us, and a watchman stood guard outside to see that nobody left. HF describes these marked doors as one of the saddest sights of the whole year, and the cries from behind them as even worse.

Many families could not bear to be locked up with the dying, and they invented every trick they could to escape, from bribing the watchman to climbing out of back windows after dark. HF tells of watchmen being sent on false errands, tricked by a noise in the next street, or even pushed aside by desperate men. The orders had been made to protect the city, but in practice they gave people a strong reason to hide their illness and to run.

In each parish old women, known as searchers, were paid to examine the dead and report what had killed them, and the figures in the Bills depended on their word. HF explains that these women were often poor, careless or open to a small bribe, and that families who dreaded the closing of their house paid them to name some other cause. For this reason, he suspects that the true number of plague deaths was far higher than the printed totals.

Convinced that dogs and cats helped to spread the infection, the city appointed men to kill them, and thousands of animals were destroyed in the streets. Modern scientists believe that fleas carried on rats were a main cause of plague, so the slaughter may have removed the natural enemies of the rats and made matters worse. HF records that vast numbers of animals were killed, yet he never claims that the plague grew any weaker because of it.

One of HF's most important observations is that the sickness does not always show itself, since a person who looks perfectly well may carry it for days and give it to everyone he meets. This explains, he thinks, why the plague spread so fast, and why careful people who shunned every visibly sick neighbour caught it all the same. It was a cruel discovery, because it meant that nobody could ever be certain of being safe in company.

As the summer heat grew fiercer, the great city became an eerie, half-empty place, with silent markets, shuttered shops and carts that no longer rumbled over the stones. HF says that grass began to grow in some of the busiest streets, while the few people who still walked about kept to the middle of the road, as far from the houses as they could. London, once so noisy that a man could not hear his own thoughts, now seemed to be listening.

With the shops shut and the ships idle, thousands of workmen, servants and sailors suddenly had no wages, and hunger followed fear into the poorest streets. HF praises the Lord Mayor and the wealthy citizens who gave large sums of money to relieve them, and he believes that without such charity the death toll would have been even worse. Even so, many of the poorest families had little to eat but what their neighbours could spare, and some had nothing at all.

Others looked for safety on the river, and soon the Thames was crowded with boats and ships, their decks packed with families who had decided that the water was their best protection. HF describes this floating town of vessels, where families lived for weeks on small boats and waited for the sickness to pass. For many it was a wise choice, because the open water was cleaner and quieter than the crowded streets, although no place was entirely safe.

Some clergymen fled with the other wealthy citizens, but a number of ministers, including some who had lost their places in the Church of England, stayed in London to preach and to comfort the dying. HF describes how the churches were half empty, with worshippers sitting far apart, and how people watched their neighbours for signs of sickness. Yet the faith of many grew stronger in these months, and he thinks that the city's grief at least taught it to pray.

Among the strange figures of that summer was Solomon Eagle, who walked the streets with a pan of burning coals upon his head, crying out in a terrible voice about the wrath of God. HF watched him pass with a mixture of pity and alarm, for the sight was enough to turn the stoutest heart cold. Whether the man was a prophet or merely a madman, he gave a face to the terror that filled the city.

The silence of the empty streets was broken by sudden cries from the windows of houses where someone had died, and HF says that the sound sometimes made his blood run cold. Preachers of doom walked the city, one of them calling out that, like Nineveh, London had only forty days left before it would be overthrown. Yet the people who heard such voices went on buying bread, nursing the sick and burying the dead, as ordinary life continued beside the horror.

As the numbers of dead grew, the parishes sent carts through the streets at night, each led by a man with a bell who called for the dead to be brought out. HF could hardly describe the effect of that sound, which came closer and closer in the darkness until it stopped outside some neighbour's house. There was neither time nor room for the old funeral customs, and the dead were carried straight to the great common graves.

When the churchyards could hold no more, the parishes dug huge common pits, and HF walked to the one beside Aldgate church to look into it with his own eyes. By his account it was some forty feet long and about fifteen feet wide, and it would soon hold hundreds of the dead. He stood in silence at the edge, filled with awe and sorrow, and left with a deeper sense of how many families had been struck.

HF retells the tale of a poor piper who, after a long evening of drinking, fell asleep in the street and was taken for dead by the men with the cart. They laid him among the bodies and drove on, until the jolting and the cold roused the sleeper, who sat up and asked in alarm where on earth he was. The carters, as frightened as he was, had to be convinced that he was alive, and the tale passed from mouth to mouth.

At its height, in the second half of September, the printed Bills recorded more than seven thousand deaths in a single week, a figure that would have been unthinkable a year before. HF is convinced that the real number was higher still, because hurried burials, bribes to the searchers and the simple chaos of the time hid many victims from the count. Behind each of those figures, he reminds us, stood a household, a family and a name that someone loved.

Those who caught the disease suffered terribly from fever and swellings, and HF describes how some, in their pain and delirium, escaped from their beds and rushed into the streets or even into the river. Neighbours who saw them could do nothing to help, for to touch them was to risk the same fate. He writes of such scenes with plain pity, and he never turns the suffering of ordinary people into a sensational spectacle.

The plague tested the bonds of love and friendship as harshly as it tested the human body, and no one could be sure how they would act. HF records that some people, in a panic, deserted their own sick relatives, while others, at great risk, stayed beside a dying neighbour and brought food, water and comfort. His verdict is balanced, for he refuses to call any group of people wholly cruel or wholly good.

Nursing the sick was left chiefly to poor women, who took the dangerous work for small pay and often caught the disease themselves. HF has heard dark stories of nurses who robbed or neglected their patients, yet he doubts that such wickedness was common, and he insists that the greater part of them did their duty bravely. Many of these women, he believes, deserve a far warmer memory than the stories of that dreadful year have usually given them.

HF now turns aside to tell of three poor men who decided that their only hope was to leave London, setting out together with their savings and a plan to live in the open country. None of them had any means except his own hands, and each had friends who thought that the journey would be foolish. HF tells their story at length, because he believes it shows how courage and common sense can survive in hard times.

At last the three companions settled at the edge of a great forest, where they built a rough shelter from branches, cloth and whatever else they could find. They kept well away from the towns, and they depended on the kindness of country people, who sometimes left bread and milk at a distance and hurried away in fear. It was a hard and lonely life, but it taught them that many people could still be generous even when they were afraid.

Fear travelled faster than the plague itself, and the towns and villages around London began to guard their roads against anyone who came from the city. Travellers were required to carry certificates of health, signed by the proper officers, and even those who held them were often turned away or forced to sleep in the fields. HF remarks that the refugees were pitied by some and cursed by others, and that no one could blame the frightened country people for protecting their families.

In one of his quieter moments, HF considers a question that troubled many people: was the plague a judgement sent by God, or simply a natural sickness spreading from person to person? He concludes that it was both, since he cannot believe that God would use anything but natural means, and that it is foolish to neglect sensible care while waiting for a miracle. This blend of deep faith and practical good sense runs through the whole book and gives its narrator his quiet authority.

It was the poor who took the greatest risks, for the watchmen, the gravediggers and the cart drivers were mostly men who had no other way to earn their bread. HF admires their steadiness, and he notes that many of them died at their posts, while others somehow survived until the last day of the plague. Their courage, he suggests, deserves a place in the story beside that of the Lord Mayor and the clergy.

Fear changed the manners of the whole city, and neighbours who had once greeted one another warmly now crossed the road to avoid a meeting. People carried bundles of herbs, bottles of perfume and bits of tobacco, and some chewed or sniffed them constantly, in the hope that the sweet smell would drive away the poison. HF watches these habits with sympathy, though he doubts that any of them offered much real protection against such a deadly enemy.

As an observer of his own city, HF notices that the plague moved like a slow tide, beginning in the west, spreading into the heart of London and rolling eastward into the crowded streets beyond the walls. In the poor, overcrowded parishes the death toll was far higher than in the wider streets of the rich, who in any case had mostly left. He draws no grand conclusion, but he records it carefully, as a witness who wants others to understand where danger lay.

Then, as the autumn air grew cool, the weekly count of the dead began, to everyone's astonishment, to fall, and the whole city looked at the figures as if they were a miracle. HF describes how people who had passed one another in silence for months stopped to share the news, and how strangers smiled for the first time in half a year. Yet the relief was cautious, because people had been disappointed before and hardly dared to trust a good week.

As the weeks went by, a remarkable change was noticed: many of those who fell ill now recovered, whereas a few weeks earlier so many had died. The physicians and surgeons argued about the cause, some crediting the colder weather, others the new treatments of the swellings, and others the simple fact that the sickness had run its course. HF, with his usual caution, declines to pick a side, and he is content to give thanks that the change had come.

Relief, however, made many people reckless, and HF watched with alarm as citizens who had hidden for months now rushed into the streets, shook hands warmly and visited houses where the sickness still lingered. A number of them fell ill again and died, just when the worst seemed to be over, and the city learned that hope without patience can be dangerous. He blames no one for the joy, but he wishes that more people had kept their caution until the danger had truly passed.

Little by little, the shutters came down from the shops, the markets filled again, and the families who had fled in the summer began to creep back to their abandoned houses. HF says that many of them were astonished to find the city still standing, and even more astonished to find so many acquaintances missing from the streets. The King and his court stayed away for some months longer, and did not return to London until early in the following year.

By the middle of winter the plague had almost vanished, though a handful of cases lingered into the new year and kept the careful people watchful. The weekly Bills, which had once been read with horror, were now read with something close to joy, and the sound of ordinary life returned slowly to the streets. London, scarred but alive, turned back to the ordinary labour of living, and it began slowly to count what it had lost.

Historians estimate that about one hundred thousand people died of the plague in London during 1665, which means that roughly one in every five Londoners lost their lives. Whole families were wiped out, whole streets emptied, and many of the poorest victims were buried without anyone knowing their names. HF reports these facts without exaggeration or complaint, for he feels that the plain numbers are heavy enough to carry their own grief.

HF himself never caught the plague, although his curiosity had carried him into some of the most dangerous streets of the city. He gives thanks for his survival, and he has the honesty to admit that he cannot explain it, since careful people and careless people alike had fallen on every side. Luck, faith and good judgement all played a part in his case, he suspects, but he never pretends to know the exact proportions.

As the danger recedes, HF offers a few pieces of plain advice to anyone who might one day meet such a disaster. He urges them to keep a store of food, to avoid crowds, to distrust every promise of a magic cure and, above all, to remain in good order and kindness toward their neighbours. A calm and well-prepared household, he believes, is the best protection that ordinary people can hope to have.

Londoners had scarcely begun to recover when, in September 1666, the Great Fire swept through the old city and destroyed most of the houses within the walls. The city was rebuilt in brick and stone, and the great plague of 1665 turned out to be the last of its kind to strike London on such a scale. Some people have wondered whether the fire cleansed the city, though historians note that the plague had already faded before the flames began.

Defoe published the Journal in 1722, when news of a terrible plague in the French port of Marseille had made the English fear that the sickness might return. He wished to remind his countrymen what a real epidemic meant, and to show them how sensible precautions might save lives. Because the book was written in such a convincing voice, many readers took it for the genuine diary of a survivor, and some historians long cited it as a primary source.

The book's lasting power lies in its refusal to make heroes and villains of its people, for its pages are crowded with ordinary men and women who are frightened, kind, selfish and brave by turns. It also shows how rumour, false cures and private panic can do almost as much damage as the disease, while honest information and steady courage save lives. That is why readers today, who have lived through epidemics of their own, still find it uncomfortably familiar.

The book closes with a short verse in which HF says that a dreadful plague swept a hundred thousand souls out of London in the year sixty-five, and that he himself was still alive. The humble rhyme gathers into a few words all the awe, sorrow and gratitude that the long journal has built up. It is the voice of an ordinary survivor who has seen too much to boast and who wishes only that others will remember.
